title: Hypertrophy Q&A #9
summary: NH answers about 50 viewer questions on hypertrophy: programming around rotating work schedules and night shifts, minimal leg volume, evolving rep ranges, trap-dominant shoulders, sneaking in calves and abs, growing while strength stalls, frequency versus bro splits, warm-ups, tempo, and why he rejects training blocks for bodybuilders. Recurring themes are tonnage, reps in reserve, consistency, and training the muscle rather than the movement.
claims: Rotation of 14 days with no gym then 7 days with a gym: use calisthenics (rings, dips, pull-ups, push-ups) to specialize the upper body with high volume and frequency for the 14 days, then hit legs three times during the 7 gym days
During the no-gym stretch keep conditioning and work capacity with very high-rep, high-frequency, short-rest lower body work like band good mornings and band squats
Three leg sessions a week with 4 heavy sets of knee flexion and 4 of hip hinge each (12 weekly sets of each) is enough, even high volume
NH does only about 6-7 heavy knee-flexion sets a week and his legs grow fine; the lower body responds well to minimalism
Taller men with long legs may need to lean toward more volume and less intensity, which lowers injury risk and builds tonnage over time
NH's legs started visibly growing after about two years of squatting 2-3 times a week, and they are still growing; natural leg potential is very high
The key to leg growth is consistency: train them 2-3 times a week for years instead of going all out for three months and burning out
If you miss your target reps on the first set of an evolving rep range, the jump was too big; go back to the previous weight next week, rebuild, and jump more carefully or widen the range
If traps take over lateral raises, use an 'Egyptian' lateral raise: hold a rack and lean the body away so the torso is tilted, which takes the traps out; NH has replaced normal lateral raises with it
Traps can't really take over the overhead press because the delts are the prime mover
Calves and abs left for the end of a session get skipped; put them in giant sets with exercises you enjoy, or train them on upper days
NH does most of his calf volume on upper days, in giant sets like overhead press, chin-ups, knee raises, then calves, done slowly so the calves also act as rest for the shoulders
Any type of resistance, kettlebells included, is valid for hypertrophy if you know how to use it; NH has no kettlebell experience
NH added only about 20 lb to his squat over the past year while his legs kept growing
Legs can grow without much strength progress through volume and damage: 10,000 lb of tonnage at 85% beats 5,000 lb at 100%
Train with reps in reserve so you can repeat the work three days later, rather than hitting the wall every session
Evolving rep ranges let him repeat weights and add sets instead of jumping in load, which suits hypertrophy; progression is still needed as proof of added muscle and for motivation
Track weights and reps on every set of every exercise, including curls, not just the main lifts
The upper back can be trained very often because it is many small muscles with different recovery times; hit it every day with varying angles

Naturally strong lifters chasing hypertrophy shouldn't fall into constant max testing; use the strength to add sets and reps, and expect a higher strength threshold before size shows (e.g. 195 lb overhead press for reps vs 135 for NH)
If a method gives an overwhelming pump but no progress, drop it

For bigger side delts: vertical press at least twice a week building toward three (two loaded, one bodyweight), face pulls at the end of every session, and lateral raises wherever they can be recovered from, with a focus on volume
Heavy shrugs and heavy farmer's walks add a weighted stretch that helps build that heavy-set shoulder look
Short clavicles won't give a dramatic V-taper but you can still build big shoulders relative to your frame
After shoulder surgery, keep training everything else and do cardio; staying sedentary for five months makes recovery worse
Heel-elevated squats are better for quad growth than regular squats for someone whose glutes dominate, even with less weight
Bro splits' real problems are low frequency and junk volume; if recovery is a problem, go minimalist with few sets per muscle and then rebuild frequency rather than adopting a bro split
Unless you're 65-70, regressing in strength and size means a problem with your program or diet, not age
Hitting a muscle three times a week only causes overuse injuries if you repeat the same exercise; train the muscle, not the movement, by rotating variations
Small per-session differences from higher frequency compound over 52 weeks and 10 years into a big difference in muscle size
A squat or deadlift stance with one foot ahead is not a problem unless it causes pain; if it is, use lighter weight to fix the hip shift and keep the single-leg work
Start evolving rep ranges on the strength work, then extend them to accessories for more control over volume and intensity
Mind-muscle connection matters mostly for muscles that struggle to grow; NH feels nothing in his legs when he squats yet they grow
Compare two exercises over three months and keep whichever gives more progress, regardless of mind-muscle connection
Don't obsess over measurement standards; leg size depends on leg length, so just train and let them grow
5x5 is too rigid and will eventually stall; when it does, switch methods rather than resetting and retrying
After a break, start with about a third of your usual tonnage; you'll regain muscle quickly, and jumping back to old loads causes injuries
Rotating out an exercise as soon as you plateau teaches you to quit and resets you to newbie neurological gains; rotate weekly by plan or autoregulate instead
Bodyweight targets depend on frame and bodyfat; at NH's height he could weigh 170 lb by dropping fat, but a 5'7 natural won't be 240 lb unless fat
The gentleman split is the proper way to do an upper/lower: mostly upper or lower work, with exceptions like calves on upper day
You can keep gaining at the same weight by adding sets and reps until it becomes junk volume, then increase the weight
Overhead press, bench, squat and deadlift are fine for hypertrophy; old-school bodybuilders grew with them and most of NH's programs are built on them
Bugenhagen isn't big from the Wisconsin max-out method; he also does a lot of volume, so daily maxes alone aren't enough
Cardio and lifting on the same day doesn't kill gains; just avoid intense leg cardio on leg days
If knee power shrugs stress the lower back, switch to normal, seated, or chest-supported incline shrugs
If poor internal rotation forces a wide, duck-footed back squat, make front squats your main squat; front squat variations alone can build big quads
Warm-up sets count as tonnage but not relevant tonnage; keep them minimal so they don't impair the work sets
NH warms up by doing the exercise with light weight and adding about 20-50 lb per set up to his working weight
Time under tension is overrated; do slow negatives to reinforce form and suffer through the lengthening, but no need to count five seconds
Night shift workers should train before work, which also wakes them up, instead of after a tiring shift
NH barely trains his shoulders, pressing about once every 15 days, because they grow too easily and he doesn't want them bigger
Bodybuilders should autoregulate rather than follow named schemes; schemes are just labels for what works
Training blocks and mesocycles come from strength sports; a bodybuilder is an artist, not an athlete, and should prefer continuous, smooth autoregulated progress over peaking
Rounded-back deadlift form and bad posture reinforce each other
In the conventional deadlift, whether your shins bleed says nothing about correct form; it depends on your build
Traps respond to higher reps; NH uses a 10-15 rep evolving range on knee power shrugs and only shows his 15-rep sets
Trading reps for weight only pays off if the heavier load is sustainable and leads to more tonnage later
If dumbbell pullovers hit the triceps more than the lats, try barbell or EZ-bar pullovers with different grips
To look big without flexing, build muscle and carry some fat so you look full at rest
Lu raises and lateral raises are equally fine; do both if you like them
Program Atlas stones as a hip hinge in hybrid strongman training and account for lower back fatigue
Beginners without direction should study the channel and good educators but mainly train consistently, recover and progress
